title: Trailing Zeros in Factorials and Products
tagline: Year 3 — Counting zeros through the powers of 5 and 2, and the highest power of a number in n!

introduction.overview: The number of trailing zeros of a number is the number of times 10 divides it. Since 10 = 2 × 5, it equals the smaller of the exponent of 2 and the exponent of 5 in the prime factorisation. In factorials and products the powers of 2 are plentiful, so the count is decided by the powers of 5. The same method gives the highest power of any number that divides n!.
introduction.placementRelevance: Trailing-zero questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually as "the number of zeros at the end of 100!" or of a given product.
introduction.realWorldContext: Counting factors in large products is used in combinatorics, probability and in sizing numbers in computing.

learningObjectives: Count trailing zeros as min(exponent of 2, exponent of 5)
Use Legendre's formula for the power of a prime in n!
Find the highest power of a composite number dividing n!
Count zeros in a product given in factored form

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The exponent of a prime p in a number N is the number of times p divides N. 10 = 2 × 5.

coreDefinitions: Trailing zeros: zeros at the end of the decimal form of a number.
Legendre's formula: the exponent of a prime p in n! is ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + …
Zeros in n! = exponent of 5 in n! (since 2s are more frequent).
For a composite m = p^a q^b …, the highest power of m dividing n! is the minimum of ⌊(exponent of p in n!)/a⌋, …
⌊x⌋ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding x.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every 10 needs one 2 and one 5. In a long product there are far more 2s than 5s, so the 5s run out first and decide the number of zeros.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Count the multiples of 5, then of 25, then of 125, and add. For a given product, write it as 2^a × 5^b × (other) and take min(a, b).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Legendre
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Power of a prime in n!.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Composite divisor
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Highest power of m^k = min over primes ⌊v_p(n!)/a⌋

mainNarrative: For n!, count the multiples of 5, 25, 125 and so on. For 100!: ⌊100/5⌋ = 20 and ⌊100/25⌋ = 4, so 24 zeros. Multiples of 25 are counted twice because each contains two 5s.
For a product in factored form, write the total powers of 2 and 5. In 2¹⁰ × 5¹² × 7, the exponent of 2 is 10 and of 5 is 12, so there are min(10, 12) = 10 trailing zeros.
Legendre's formula works for any prime. In 50!, the exponent of 3 is ⌊50/3⌋ + ⌊50/9⌋ + ⌊50/27⌋ = 16 + 5 + 1 = 22.
For the highest power of a composite number, split it into primes. For 12 = 2² × 3 in 50!, v₂ = 25 + 12 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 47 so 47 ÷ 2 → 23, and v₃ = 22, so the highest power of 12 is the smaller, 22.
Mixed products: 25⁶ × 4⁶ = (25 × 4)⁶ = 100⁶, which has 12 zeros. 15 × 15 × … products need the exponents of 5 and 2 separately.

deepDiveAspects.title: Count the 5s, not the 2s
deepDiveAspects.content: In a factorial there are always at least as many 2s as 5s, so counting 5s is enough. In an arbitrary product this is not guaranteed; always compute both.

deepDiveAspects.title: Zeros in the exact numbers
deepDiveAspects.content: A number ends in exactly k zeros if 10^k divides it and 10^(k+1) does not.

solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using only the exponent of 3 without dividing 2s by 2.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Divide n by 5, then divide the quotient by 5 again, and add the quotients until the quotient is 0.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Dividing the exponent of the larger prime.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Divide each prime's exponent by its power in m.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The number of zeros in n! is about n/4; reject options far from this.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the repeated division by 5 in a column.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The same Legendre sum answers most "highest power" questions.
